name: Tsonga
confidence_why: Junod 1907 and Ouwehand 1965 both place the accent on the penultimate syllable, and Selkirk 2011 (after Kisseberth 1994) and Lee and Riedel 2022 find the same penultimate prominence, though they describe it as phrase-edge lengthening rather than word stress, so the placement is uncontested while its word-level status rests on two older grammars.

new_statements.quote: 23. The accent is well marked. It falls on the penultimate, when the word is polysyllabic (except in the locative case and the imperative mood where it falls on the last syllable). Monosyllabic words have generally no accent. Some have it always (as the conjunction ke (§ 244) and the descriptive adverbs (§ 226). Others take it when followed by other monosyllables forming with them a kind of phonetic unity. Ex. muti wa nga. The village of me. 24. There are also slight differences of intonation which allow a trained ear to distinguish between words otherwise identical. For instance, the word matimba means both strength and pieces of sugar-cane. In both cases the accent is on the penultimate. But there is a second accent on the last when it means strength.
new_statements.citation: Junod, Henri A. 1907. Elementary grammar of the Thonga-Shangaan language. Lausanne: Georges Bridel. [NOT in the 'works' list; held by the project in the language folder from the 2026-09-16 pass]
new_statements.locator: Part I, IV 'Syllabic System and Accentuation', § 23-24, pp. 11-12 (pp. 15-16); also § 2, p. 7 (p. 11)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: lines 508-531: '23. The accent is well marked. It falls on the penulti-mate, when the word is polysyllabic (except in the locative [page break, printed '12'] cast' and the imperative mood where it falls on the last syllable). Monosyllabic words have generally no accent. Some have it always (as the conjunction ke (§ 244) and the descriptive adverbs (§ 226). Others take it when followed by other monosyllables forming with them a kind of pho-netic unity. Ex. muti wa nga. The village of me. 24. There are also slight differences of intonation which allow a trained ear to distinguish between wo]*ds other-wise identical. For instance, the word matimba means both strength and pieces of sugar-cane.…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate: penultimate stress); adds the penultimate-length correlate, the final-accent exceptions in locatives and imperatives, and the treatment of monosyllables. Describes 'Thonga-Shangaan' (Junod's Mozambique/Transvaal Thonga, the same language).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word; the penultimate vowel is generally long. Exceptions: the locative case of nouns and the imperative mood, where the accent moves to the final syllable (these are the forms that drop the final vowel and end in -en/-in). Monosyllables are generally unaccented unless grouped with other monosyllables into a phonetic unit or lexically accented (ke, descriptive adverbs). A 'second accent' on the final syllable distinguishes a few otherwise identical words (matimba 'strength' vs 'pieces of sugar-cane'), which is a tonal distinction described in accentual terms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'second accent' on the final syllable in some words (§ 24, p. 12: matimba 'strength' vs 'sugar-cane pieces'; shirimi pair) - lexical, i.e. a tone difference; no regular secondary stress described.
new_statements.exceptions: Locative case and imperative mood take final accent (§ 23, p. 11; § 53 note p. ~35: 'the accent being moved from the penultimate to the last syllable'); monosyllables generally unaccented; monosyllabic verbs add a syllable in the imperative 'evidently on account of the accentuation' (tana 'come').
new_statements.identity_note: Junod 1907 describes 'Thonga-Shangaan' (the Ronga/Djonga-influenced Mozambican-Transvaal variety of the Swiss Mission); Ouwehand 1965 is a pedagogical grammar of South African Tsonga; Selkirk 2011 uses Kisseberth's Xitsonga data (northeast South Africa and Mozambique); Lee & Riedel 2022 record South African Xitsonga speakers. All are the same language (tson1249); no dialect-specific stress difference is claimed by any of them.

new_statements.quote: D. Accentuation and Intonation. Usually the accent in the word is on the last syllable but one (the penultimate). Note that a syllable always ends with a vowel: Xi - kwe - mbu: Xikwembu — God; ri - rha - ndzu: rirhandzu — love. Apart from the accent, the intonation of a word or sentence is very important in Tsonga. Every word has its own intonation, and when it is not pronounced with its right intonation, it is pronounced wrongly.
new_statements.citation: Ouwehand, M. 1965. Everyday Tsonga. (archive.org copy; publisher not verified from the copy) [NOT in the 'works' list; held by the project in the language folder from the 2026-09-16 pass]
new_statements.locator: Introduction, § D 'Accentuation and Intonation', pp. 11-12 (pp. 14-15); footnote p. 78 (p. 81)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: lines 477-486: 'D. Accentuation and Intonation. Usually the accent in the word is on the last syllable but one (the penultimate). Note that a syllable always ends with a vowel: - kwe - mbu: Xikwembu — God / ri - rha - ndzu : rirhandzu — love / Apart from the accent, the intonation of a word or sentence is very important in Tsonga. Every word has its own intonation, and when it is not pronounced with its right intonation, it is pronounced [marker '12 EVERYDAY TSONGA'] wrongly.' Verbatim (the scanned drops the 'Xi' of the first syllabification). The passage starts on p. 11 and its last word falls on p. 12, so 'pp. 11-12' is right; p. 12 continues: 'the intonation is dependent on the situation…
new_statements.relation_note: Penultimate accent, as in the catalog; a pedagogical grammar, not a scientific description (its own preface says so). Also states the language is tonal, with tone patterns dependent on sentence position.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is usually on the penultimate syllable; separately, every word has a tone pattern ('intonation') that depends on its position in the sentence. A footnote notes that the shortened possessive 'wavo' is pronounced with stress and a long vowel on the final -vo because it stands for 'vona'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Usually' - hedged; fn. p. 78: 'tata wavo would be pronounced with the stress on "vo" (with a long vowel), this being considered the short form of "vona"' (a truncated form keeps its original penult stress, hence surface final stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Junod 1907 describes 'Thonga-Shangaan' (the Ronga/Djonga-influenced Mozambican-Transvaal variety of the Swiss Mission); Ouwehand 1965 is a pedagogical grammar of South African Tsonga; Selkirk 2011 uses Kisseberth's Xitsonga data (northeast South Africa and Mozambique); Lee & Riedel 2022 record South African Xitsonga speakers. All are the same language (tson1249); no dialect-specific stress difference is claimed by any of them.

new_statements.quote: In Xitsonga, all and only vowels that are penultimate in the clause are long (V:). There is no lexical vowel length contrast; this penultimate lengthening is introduced by the phonology. According to a purely syntactic approach, the clause would constitute the phonological domain for penultimate lengthening. But according to the prosodic structure hypothesis, and specifically Match theory, (4), the clause would correspond to an intonational phrase, or ι-domain, which itself would be the domain for penultimate lengthening
new_statements.citation: Selkirk, Elisabeth. 2011. The syntax-phonology interface. In J. Goldsmith, J. Riggle & A. Yu (eds.), The Handbook of Phonological Theory, 2nd ed. Oxford: Blackwell (pre-print 'corrected 2/2011'). [NOT in the 'works' list; held by the project in the language folder from the 2026-09-16 pass]
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: lines 273-280 (= p. 6, footer '6', § 2.1.1 'Penultimate lengthening'): 'In Xitsonga, all and only vowels that are penultimate in the clause are long (V:). There is no lexical vowel length contrast; this penultimate lengthening is introduced by the phonology11. According to a purely syntactic approach, the clause would constitute the phonological domain for penultimate lengthening. But according to the prosodic structure hypothesis, and specifically Match theory, (4), the clause would correspond to an intonational phrase, or ι-domain, which itself would be the domain for penultimate lengthening' - verbatim apart from the footnote numeral. p. 6 also: 'In Xitsonga, a Bantu language of northeas…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate placement in the sense that the prominence-bearing position is the penult, but the work locates it at the clause/intonational-phrase level, not the word; it does not claim word stress. Data are Kisseberth's Xitsonga (South Africa / Mozambique).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Xitsonga has no lexical vowel length; the penultimate vowel of the clause (intonational phrase) is lengthened by the phonology, and this penultimate lengthening (plus high-tone spread) diagnoses phrase edges. The work says nothing about word-level stress as such; the penultimate prominence it describes is a property of the intonational phrase (based on Kisseberth 1994 and Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1998).
new_statements.exceptions: Postposed subjects and preposed objects carry their own penultimate lengthening (separate ι-domains), pp. 6-9.
new_statements.identity_note: Junod 1907 describes 'Thonga-Shangaan' (the Ronga/Djonga-influenced Mozambican-Transvaal variety of the Swiss Mission); Ouwehand 1965 is a pedagogical grammar of South African Tsonga; Selkirk 2011 uses Kisseberth's Xitsonga data (northeast South Africa and Mozambique); Lee & Riedel 2022 record South African Xitsonga speakers. All are the same language (tson1249); no dialect-specific stress difference is claimed by any of them.

new_statements.quote: PL in Xitsonga is reported to mark the boundary of an intonational phrase (Kisseberth 1994, Selkirk 2011). Whether or not penultimate syllables of the lower prosodic levels (phonological phrases and prosodic words) are also realised as lengthened vowels has not been reported. Anecdotally, one of the authors of this paper reports that PL is heard at the prosodic word level in naturalistic conversation amongst native speakers of Xitsonga. [fn. 1, p. 108:] No systematic study reports word-level PL in Xitsonga. However, such lengthening has been reported for other Bantu languages, as noted below.
new_statements.citation: Lee, Seunghun J. & Kristina Riedel. 2022. Pre-nominal DP modifiers and penultimate lengthening in Xitsonga. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 62: 107-134. doi:10.5842/62-0-907 [NOT in the 'works' list; held by the project in the language folder from the 2026-09-16 pass; companion to the unopened 2023 paper]
new_statements.locator: § 1 fn. 1, p. 108; § 4 'Phonetic evidence for Xitsonga PL', p. 117
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: lines 513-517 (p. 11 = printed p. 117, under '4. Phonetic evidence for Xitsonga PL'): 'PL in Xitsonga is reported to mark the boundary of an intonational phrase (Kisseberth 1994, Selkirk 2011). Whether or not penultimate syllables of the lower prosodic levels (phonological phrases and prosodic words) are also realised as lengthened vowels has not been reported. Anecdotally, one of the authors of this paper reports that PL is heard at the prosodic word level in naturalistic conversation amongst native speakers of Xitsonga.' and fn. 1 (line 96, printed p. 108): 'No systematic study reports word-level PL in Xitsonga. However, such lengthening has been reported for other Bantu languages, as not…
new_statements.relation_note: Does not contradict the penultimate record but weakens its word-level basis: the instrumental literature treats the penultimate prominence as a phrase-edge lengthening effect, with word-level penultimate lengthening 'not reported' systematically. Data from Xitsonga speakers in South Africa (Univ. of Venda / Free State).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Penultimate lengthening (PL) in Xitsonga is reported to mark the right edge of the intonational phrase; whether the penult of every prosodic word is lengthened has not been systematically reported (one author hears word-level PL in conversation). Their measurements find graded PL: longest at intonational-phrase edges, shorter at focused phonological-phrase edges. No claim about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-level penultimate lengthening is unreported/anecdotal (fn. 1 p. 108; § 4 p. 117); PL is graded by prosodic level (IP-final longest, PP-final shorter, focused PP-final longer than unfocused), p. 117.
new_statements.identity_note: Junod 1907 describes 'Thonga-Shangaan' (the Ronga/Djonga-influenced Mozambican-Transvaal variety of the Swiss Mission); Ouwehand 1965 is a pedagogical grammar of South African Tsonga; Selkirk 2011 uses Kisseberth's Xitsonga data (northeast South Africa and Mozambique); Lee & Riedel 2022 record South African Xitsonga speakers. All are the same language (tson1249); no dialect-specific stress difference is claimed by any of them.

new_statements.quote: Xitsonga, like the vast majority of Bantu languages, is a tone language that also makes extensive use of penultimate lengthening to mark phrase boundaries (Kisseberth 1994). High (H) tone spreading and lengthening of penultimate vowels are important markers of phonological phrase boundaries. [p. 7] ... Although the application of NON-FINALITY at different levels displays different H tone spreading patterns, the penultimate lengthening pattern holds in both dialects. Only the penultimate syllable before a higher prosodic phrase boundary is lengthened. [p. 9]
new_statements.citation: Lee, Seunghun J., Kristina Riedel & al. 2023. Recursivity and Focus in the Prosody of Xitsonga DPs. Languages 8(2): 150. doi:10.3390/languages8020150
new_statements.locator: Section 2 'Prosodic Phrasing in Xitsonga', p. 7 of 19 (tone language + penultimate lengthening statement); p. 9 (dialect note on PL); also sec. 1 pp. 5-6 and sec. 4.1 p. 13
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File is the genuine MDPI publisher PDF (the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Recursivity and Focus in the Prosody of Xitsonga DPs', Author 'Seunghun Lee and Kristina Riedel', pdfTeX, 19 pp., 448,213 B, created 2023-06-09); has the download line (mdpi-res.com CDN). In the extracted text the first quoted passage is at line 409ff, opening Section 2 'Prosodic Phrasing in Xitsonga', on page 7 of 19 (form-feed count and running header '7 of 19' at line 382): 'Xitsonga, like the vast majority of Bantu languages, is a tone language that also makes extensive use of penultimate lengthening to mark phrase boundaries (Kisseberth 1994). High (H) tone spreading and lengthening of penultimate vowels are im…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate record (penultimate stress = penult) in that the locus of prominence is the penultimate syllable, but the work frames it as phrase-level penultimate vowel lengthening before a higher prosodic boundary in a tone language, not as word stress; it neither asserts nor denies word-level stress, so it adds domain (phrase-final / focus-phrase) and type (lengthening in a tonal system) detail rather than a different placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Xitsonga is described as a tone language (unbounded H-tone spreading, blocked from the phrase-final syllable by Non-Finality); the only prominence-like property discussed is penultimate lengthening, which the authors treat as a marker of a higher prosodic phrase boundary (phi-max / intonational phrase) and, in fronted DP modifiers, of a focus-marked phonological phrase. The word 'stress' does not occur in the paper; no statement is made about word-level stress placement or its absence.
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate lengthening also appears in non-final position on a DP modifier fronted to FocP (focus-marked phi), but not on scrambled modifiers or on 'hinkwa-wo' + noun; H-tone spreading differs by dialect (Mozambican Xitsonga per Kisseberth 1994 stops at the phrase-penult, Mhinga-area dialect may spread to the phrase-final syllable), while the penultimate-lengthening pattern is said to hold in both.
new_statements.identity_note: Lee & Riedel 2023's data come from one male native-speaker consultant in his late 40s from Giyani, Limpopo, South Africa (South African Xitsonga); the paper contrasts H-tone spreading in Mozambican Xitsonga (Kisseberth 1994) with a Mhinga-area (Limpopo) dialect and states the penultimate-lengthening pattern holds in both.

tone_statements.citation: Langa, David Alberto Seth. 2021. Wumpfumumphatu wa XiChangana: wujondzi la mpimu wa mpfumawulu, wuhangalaki ni wutsemerisi la wona / Fonologia prosódica do xiChangana: uma análise do tom, sua propagação e restrições. Njinga & Sepé: Revista Internacional de Culturas, Línguas Africanas e Brasileiras 1(Especial): 255-271.
tone_statements.quote: O Changana é uma língua tonal e, por isso, é relevante que o trabalho fixe os padrões tonais da mesma. ... Os dados em (27) mostram, claramente, que o Changana é uma língua com dois tons básicos, que se distribuem de formas diferentes nos nomes. ... Em resumo, a descrição do tom permite concluir o seguinte: (i) Esta língua tem 2 tons de nível, a saber, tom alto e tom baixo. (ii) O tom pode ser lexical ou gramatical; (iii) O tom alto pode propagar-se para as moras seguintes até a penúltima sílaba. (iv) A propagação do tom alto é bloqueada quando a palavra seguinte tiver o tom lexical contrastivo.
tone_statements.translation: Changana is a tone language and it is therefore relevant that this work fix its tonal patterns. ... The data in (27) show clearly that Changana is a language with two basic tones, which are distributed in different ways in nouns. ... In sum, the description of tone allows the following conclusions: (i) This language has 2 level tones, namely high tone and low tone. (ii) Tone may be lexical or grammatical; (iii) High tone may spread to the following moras up to the penultimate syllable. (iv) High-tone spreading is blocked when the following word has contrastive lexical tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 4.4 'Tom em Changana': p. 79, p. 82 and the summary on p. 92
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones H/L, lexical and grammatical; only L marked (grave); H spreads rightward to the penult mora of the phrase; author denies consonant (depressor) effects; contours rare, from V+V.

tone_statements.citation: Beuchat, P.-D. 1962. Additional notes on the tonomorphology of the Tsonga noun. African Studies 21: 105-122. doi:10.1080/00020186208707162
tone_statements.quote: O XiChangana é uma língua tonal em que o tom, tal como nas demais línguas bantu, caracteriza-se pela sua propagação (Liphola, 2001; Ngunga, 2014; Kenstowicz, 2020). [...] XiChangana tem basicamente dois tons, nomeadamente, o tom de nível alto e o tom de nível baixo. [...] [Resumo:] os dados analisados do tom permitem concluir que esta língua tem 2 tons de nível, a saber, tom alto e tom baixo, podendo este ser lexical ou gramatical. O tom alto pode propagar-se para as moras seguintes até a penúltima sílaba, sendo que a sua propagação é bloqueada em palavras com o tom lexical contrastivo.
tone_statements.translation: XiChangana is a tone language in which tone, as in the other Bantu languages, is characterised by its spreading. [...] XiChangana has basically two tones, namely the high level tone and the low level tone. [...] [Abstract:] the tone data analysed allow the conclusion that this language has 2 level tones, high and low, which may be lexical or grammatical. The high tone can spread to the following moras up to the penultimate syllable, its spreading being blocked in words with contrastive lexical tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Tom em XiChangana', pp. 256-257; abstract p. 255
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 (H, L); H spreads rightward to the penult

tone_statements.citation: Beuchat, P.-D. [Cole] (1959). Tonomorphology of the Tsonga noun. African studies 18. pp. 133-145.
tone_statements.quote: First, there is no H tone spread within the noun root itself. The association of H tone to tone-bearing unit is contrastive in nouns in Xitsonga; lexical H tone span may appear on any tbu of a noun in the input representation PI, including the final syllable. ... In Xitsonga nouns, a lexical H tone span may fall on one or more tone-bearing units in a noun, regardless of position, while lexical H tone in verb roots in Xitsonga is restricted to root-initial position.
tone_statements.locator: preprint p. 29, §2.2 'Generalizing to other syntactic contexts', and fn. 22 (continued on p. 30)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical H vs toneless syllables (no L tone posited); H spreads rightward, blocked at the left edge of binary phrases and by the OCP; second of two H spans downstepped (fn. 11, 21). No tone count.

tone_statements.citation: Jacques, [Révérend] A. A. (1941). Shangana-Thonga ideophones and their tones. Bantu studies 15. pp. 205-244.
tone_statements.quote: Xitsonga, a Southern Bantu language spoken primarily in South Africa, as well as in parts of Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Eswatini, possesses a complex tonal system that plays a crucial role in both lexical and grammatical distinctions.8 As a two-tone language, Xitsonga differentiates between high and low tones, with these tonal variations significantly influencing the meaning of the word.9 The interaction between high and low tones, as well as their rising and falling contours, can also result in words with entirely distinct meanings.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2890, Introduction, 2nd paragraph; footnotes 8-9 = Lee & Burheni 2014
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, high vs low; rising/falling named only as contours of H and L. Desktop study from dictionaries plus author's native-speaker intuition, e.g. nsélé 'cruelty' vs nsèlè 'hole'; no TBU/downstep.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts the catalog's penultimate placement, but the sources differ on the level at which the penultimate prominence lives. The two descriptive grammars (Junod 1907 pp. 11-12; Ouwehand 1965 p. 11) state a word-level penultimate accent, with Junod adding final accent in locatives and imperatives and unaccented monosyllables. The modern prosodic literature (Selkirk 2011 p. 6, following Kisseberth 1994; Lee & Riedel 2022 pp. 108, 117) treats the penultimate prominence as phrase-final penultimate lengthening (intonational-phrase edge), with word-level penultimate lengthening explicitly 'not reported' systematically and only anecdotal; none of these works claims or denies word stress. All sources agree the language is tonal (Junod's 'second accent' pairs, Ouwehand's 'intonation', Lee 2009's H-spread). The listed 2023 Lee & Riedel paper could not be opened (MDPI/Akamai 403 on both attempts).

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in Junod 1907 sec. 23 (pp. 11-12), now saved locally (no file was held before). Deciding source is a 1907 missionary elementary grammar, not the best available description, but every source opened agrees on penultimate prominence: Ouwehand 1965 pp. 11-12 ('accent.. on the last syllable but one'), Junod sec. 2 (penultimate vowel long and accented), Selkirk 2011 after Kisseberth 1994 (all and only clause-penultimate vowels long, no lexical length), Lee & Riedel 2022 (instrumental; PL marks right edge of prosodic word/phonological phrase/IP, longest IP-finally, word-level PL not systematically established). Junod's final-accent exceptions (locative, imperative) follow from his apocopated 1907 spellings (-en, -n for modern -eni, -ani) and do not disturb 'fixed-dominant penultimate' (not in the strict set). sources.quote: O Changana é uma língua tonal e, por isso, é relevante que o trabalho fixe os padrões tonais da mesma. ... Os dados em (27) mostram, claramente, que o Changana é uma língua com dois tons básicos, que se distribuem de formas diferentes nos nomes. ... Em resumo, a descrição do tom permite concluir o seguinte: (i) Esta língua tem 2 tons de nível, a saber, tom alto e tom baixo. (ii) O tom pode ser lexical ou gramatical; (iii) O tom alto pode propagar-se para as moras seguintes até a penúltima sílaba. (iv) A propagação do tom alto é bloqueada quando a palavra seguinte tiver o tom lexical contrastivo.

sources.note: Two level tones H/L, lexical and grammatical; only L marked (grave); H spreads rightward to the penult mora of the phrase; author denies consonant (depressor) effects; contours rare, from V+V.

tone.locator: sec. 4.4 'Tom em Changana': p. 79, p. 82 and the summary on p. 92
tone.translation: Changana is a tone language and it is therefore relevant that this work fix its tonal patterns. ... The data in (27) show clearly that Changana is a language with two basic tones, which are distributed in different ways in nouns. ... In sum, the description of tone allows the following conclusions: (i) This language has 2 level tones, namely high tone and low tone. (ii) Tone may be lexical or grammatical; (iii) High tone may spread to the following moras up to the penultimate syllable. (iv) High-tone spreading is blocked when the following word has contrastive lexical tone.

tone.quote: O XiChangana é uma língua tonal em que o tom, tal como nas demais línguas bantu, caracteriza-se pela sua propagação (Liphola, 2001; Ngunga, 2014; Kenstowicz, 2020). [...] XiChangana tem basicamente dois tons, nomeadamente, o tom de nível alto e o tom de nível baixo. [...] [Resumo:] os dados analisados do tom permitem concluir que esta língua tem 2 tons de nível, a saber, tom alto e tom baixo, podendo este ser lexical ou gramatical. O tom alto pode propagar-se para as moras seguintes até a penúltima sílaba, sendo que a sua propagação é bloqueada em palavras com o tom lexical contrastivo.
tone.locator: sec. 2 'Tom em XiChangana', pp. 256-257; abstract p. 255
tone.translation: XiChangana is a tone language in which tone, as in the other Bantu languages, is characterised by its spreading. [...] XiChangana has basically two tones, namely the high level tone and the low level tone. [...] [Abstract:] the tone data analysed allow the conclusion that this language has 2 level tones, high and low, which may be lexical or grammatical. The high tone can spread to the following moras up to the penultimate syllable, its spreading being blocked in words with contrastive lexical tone.
tone.n_tones: 2 (H, L); H spreads rightward to the penult
tone.says: First-hand tone analysis: XiChangana is a tone language with two level tones, H and L, lexical and grammatical; tonal minimal pairs (bòtà vs bótà etc.); sources of grammatical H (subject concords, 3rd-person markers, verbal copula, final-vowel H); H spreads rightward across moras up to the penult and is blocked by a contrastive lexical H; L does not spread; contra Beuchat 1961, consonant type (prenasalised/aspirated/lateral) does not block H spread in present-day Changana; noun-class prefixes a…

tone.quote: First, there is no H tone spread within the noun root itself. The association of H tone to tone-bearing unit is contrastive in nouns in Xitsonga; lexical H tone span may appear on any tbu of a noun in the input representation PI, including the final syllable. ... In Xitsonga nouns, a lexical H tone span may fall on one or more tone-bearing units in a noun, regardless of position, while lexical H tone in verb roots in Xitsonga is restricted to root-initial position.

tone.quote: Xitsonga, a Southern Bantu language spoken primarily in South Africa, as well as in parts of Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Eswatini, possesses a complex tonal system that plays a crucial role in both lexical and grammatical distinctions.8 As a two-tone language, Xitsonga differentiates between high and low tones, with these tonal variations significantly influencing the meaning of the word.9 The interaction between high and low tones, as well as their rising and falling contours, can also result in words with entirely distinct meanings.
tone.locator: p. 2890, Introduction, 2nd paragraph; footnotes 8-9 = Lee & Burheni 2014
tone.summary: Two tones, high vs low; rising/falling named only as contours of H and L. Desktop study from dictionaries plus author's native-speaker intuition, e.g. nsélé 'cruelty' vs nsèlè 'hole'; no TBU/downstep.
